item.title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Agonists or Tezepelumab for Obesity-Associated Asthma: A Cohort Study
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Obesity is associated with poor asthma outcomes. GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists induce weight loss and dampen airway inflammation independent of pathways currently targeted by biologics.

Objective: To compare differences in respiratory outcomes and weight loss between GLP-1-based medications and tezepelumab in asthma patients without diabetes.

Methods: A retrospective study was performed in a multi-institutional electronic health record database. Patients with specialist-treated, obesity-associated, moderate-to-severe asthma with at least one severe exacerbation in the prior year who initiated liraglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, or tezepelumab between January 1, 2022 and December 31, 2025 were identified. Prevalent diabetes was excluded. Patients were followed for subsequent exacerbations, rescue inhaler prescriptions, respiratory-related healthcare encounters, and time to greater than 10% loss in body mass index. Overlap weighting accounted for imbalance in baseline asthma and obesity characteristics.

Results: 2779 patients were identified, of whom 133 initiated liraglutide, 1770 semaglutide, 472 tirzepatide, and 404 tezepelumab. In weighted estimates, patients starting tirzepatide experienced a lower hazard of severe exacerbation compared to tezepelumab (weighted hazard ratio [wHR] 0.41; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.24-0.70); those starting semaglutide had a similar hazard (wHR 0.99; 95% CI 0.70-1.39). Tirzepatide and semaglutide initiators attained >10% reduction in BMI sooner, had less need for rescue inhalers, and had fewer subsequent respiratory-related encounters compared to tezepelumab.

Conclusions: GLP-1-based medications, and in particular dual-incretin GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists, may have comparable effectiveness to biologic therapy among patients with associated obesity without diabetes. Clinical trials are necessary to validate findings in this observational study.

Staggers KA, Minard C, McCormack MC, Cahill KN, Wu TD

item.title: Charcot-Leyden crystals drive a localized inflammatory niche around mucus plugs in Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Mucus plugging causes airflow obstruction, morbidity, and mortality in chronic respiratory diseases. Charcot-Leyden crystals (CLCs), formed from eosinophil-derived Galectin-10, are frequently observed in pathologic mucus, but their role in disease is unclear.

Objectives: To define the prevalence, inflammatory context, and functional role of CLCs in mucus plugs, using acute allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) as a model of eosinophilic muco-obstructive disease.

Methods: Airway samples from 19 patients with acute ABPA and 61 disease controls were analyzed for CLCs and Galectin-10. Paired samples from plugged and unplugged bronchial mucosal biopsies defined the spatial relationship between CLCs and inflammation. A novel mouse model demonstrated the contribution of CLCs to airway obstruction and inflammation and enabled evaluation of CLC-directed imaging and therapy.

Measurements and main results: Airway CLCs were a sensitive and specific marker of acute ABPA. CLC-containing mucus plugs were surrounded by a localized type 2 inflammatory niche, alongside eosinophils, neutrophils and extracellular traps, whereas inflammation was minimal in unplugged airways from the same patients, or plugs lacking CLCs. In mice, CLC-containing plugs induced persistent airway obstruction and local inflammation, both reduced by a crystal-dissolving anti-Galectin-10 antibody. Galectin-10 concentrations provided a quantitative biomarker of acute ABPA, while a CLC-targeted positron emission tomography tracer enabled noninvasive visualization of crystal-rich plugs.

Conclusions: CLC-containing mucus plugs form focal inflammatory niches in acute ABPA, and experimental CLC deposition is sufficient to promote persistent airway obstruction and inflammation. These findings identify CLCs as a biomarker, imaging target, and tractable therapeutic target in eosinophilic muco-obstructive airway disease.

item.title: The Effect of Telemedicine-Based APAP Management on 24-Hour Ambulatory Blood Pressure in Patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Telemedicine improves access to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) care, but whether telemedicine-based auto-adjusting positive airway pressure (APAP) management is noninferior to in-person care for the 3-month change in 24-hour mean blood pressure (BP) remains uncertain.

Objectives: To determine whether comprehensive telemedicine-based APAP management is noninferior to standard in-person care in reducing 24-hour mean BP in patients with OSA.

Methods: In this prospective, randomized non-inferiority trial, 344 participants with suspected OSA were randomized 1:1 to telemedicine-based (TM) or in-person (IP) management for 3 months. The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in 24-hour mean BP. The prespecified non-inferiority margin was 1.5 mmHg. Secondary outcomes included APAP adherence, patient-centered outcomes and metabolic parameters.

Measurements and main results: Of 344 randomized participants, 256 completed the 3-month follow-up (127 IP and 129 TM). The between-group difference (TM - IP) in the change in 24-hour mean BP was -0.59 mmHg (95% CI, -2.42 to 1.25) in the intention-to-treat analysis and -1.21 mmHg (95% CI, -3.24 to 0.81) in the completer analysis. Both upper confidence limits were below the prespecified 1.5-mmHg non-inferiority margin. No clear evidence of between-group differences was observed in APAP adherence, patient-reported outcomes, or metabolic measures.

Conclusions: Telemedicine-based APAP management was noninferior to in-person management for the 3-month change in 24-hour mean BP, using a prespecified margin of 1.5 mmHg. These findings support telemedicine as a potential alternative delivery model for blood pressure management in patients with OSA.

Yi H, Dong X, Zhang C, Li Z, Yang W, Zuo Y
